decks.title: Electrical Power and Energy — Part 1: Power, energy and bills
goals: Derive and use W = VIt = I²Rt = V²t/R and P = VI = I²R = V²/R
Interpret a power rating such as 1000 W, 220 V
Use the kilowatt hour and calculate the cost of electricity for a household

slides.heading: Where do the units on the bill come from?
slides.body_md: Part 1 — every appliance converts electrical energy at its own rate. The bill counts that energy in **units** (kilowatt hours).

visual.alt: Table of four household appliances, their ratings and the form of energy they produce

slides.narration: Namaste! Look at the label on any appliance at home and you will see two numbers, a power in watts and a voltage. In this part we find out what these numbers mean, how much electrical energy an appliance uses, and how that energy turns into the units that appear on your family’s electricity bill.

slides.heading: Electrical energy
slides.body_md: When a charge Q moves through a p.d. V, the work done is $W = QV$. Since $Q = It$, $W = VIt$. Using $V = IR$: $W = I^{2}Rt$; using $I = V/R$: $W = \dfrac{V^{2}t}{R}$. In a resistor all this energy becomes **heat** (Joule’s law of heating: $H = I^{2}Rt$). SI unit: **joule**.

visual.alt: Flow deriving the three forms of electrical energy from W equals Q V

slides.narration: The energy given by the supply is the charge times the potential difference. Since charge is current times time, energy is voltage times current times time. Using Ohm’s law, the same energy can be written as current squared times resistance times time, or voltage squared times time divided by resistance. In a heater all of it becomes heat.

slides.heading: Electrical power
slides.body_md: **Electrical power** is the rate at which electrical energy is converted: $P = \dfrac{W}{t} = VI = I^{2}R = \dfrac{V^{2}}{R}$. SI unit **watt (W)**: 1 W = 1 J s⁻¹; 1 kW = 1000 W. Use $P = I^{2}R$ when the **current** is common (series), and $P = \dfrac{V^{2}}{R}$ when the **voltage** is common (parallel, mains).

visual.alt: Table of the three power formulae with an example of each

slides.narration: Power is how fast energy is converted, measured in watts, where one watt is one joule every second. Power equals voltage times current. With Ohm’s law it also equals current squared times resistance, or voltage squared divided by resistance. Choose the form that uses what you know. For mains appliances the voltage is fixed, so voltage squared over resistance is handy.

slides.heading: What a power rating means
slides.body_md: A rating **“1000 W, 220 V”** on a geyser means: **when connected to 220 V, it converts 1000 J of electrical energy every second**. From the rating: $I = \dfrac{P}{V} \approx 4.55$ A and $R = \dfrac{V^{2}}{P} = 48.4$ Ω. If the supply voltage falls, R stays the same but $P = \dfrac{V^{2}}{R}$ falls **with the square of the voltage**.

functions.label: geyser element, R = 48.4 Ω: P = V² ÷ R

visual.alt: Graph of power against supply voltage for a geyser element of resistance forty eight point four ohms. The curve rises steeply: at two hundred and twenty volts the power is one thousand watts, but at one hundred and seventy six volts it is only six hundred and forty watts.
visual.caption: Power ∝ V² for a fixed resistance: a 20% fall in voltage cuts the power by 36%.

slides.narration: A rating of one thousand watts at two hundred and twenty volts means the geyser converts one thousand joules each second when it gets its proper voltage. From these two numbers you can find its current and its resistance. Its resistance stays fixed, so if the voltage drops, the power drops much faster, because power depends on the voltage squared.

slides.heading: Worked example: a geyser on a low voltage
slides.body_md:
**Problem.** A geyser is rated 1000 W, 220 V. Find (a) its resistance, (b) the current at the rated voltage, (c) its power when the supply falls to 176 V.

**(a)** $R = \dfrac{V^{2}}{P} = \dfrac{220 \times 220}{1000} = 48.4$ Ω.

**(b)** $I = \dfrac{P}{V} = \dfrac{1000}{220} \approx 4.55$ A.

**(c)** $P = \dfrac{176 \times 176}{48.4} = 640$ W.

visual.alt: Table of the geyser’s power at the rated and the reduced voltage

slides.narration: First find the resistance from the rating: two hundred and twenty squared, divided by one thousand, is forty eight point four ohms. At the rated voltage the current is about four and a half amperes. When the voltage falls to four fifths of its value, the power falls to sixteen twenty fifths, which is six hundred and forty watts.

slides.heading: Quick check: resistance from a rating
slides.body_md: Find the resistance of an appliance from its power rating.
slides.narration: Quick check. Resistance equals the voltage squared divided by the rated power.

slides.heading: Higher power, lower resistance
slides.body_md: For appliances made for the **same voltage**, $R = \dfrac{V^{2}}{P}$: the **higher the rated power, the lower the resistance**. With two equal heater coils on the mains: in **series** (resistance 2R) the power is **half** that of one coil; in **parallel** (resistance R/2) it is **double** that of one coil — **four times** the series setting.

visual.alt: Table of the power of two forty four ohm heater coils used singly, in series and in parallel on two hundred and twenty volts

slides.narration: On the same mains voltage, a more powerful appliance has a smaller resistance, because power is voltage squared divided by resistance. A heater with two equal coils can be switched to give three settings. Both coils in series give the lowest power. One coil gives twice that. Both in parallel give the highest power, four times the series setting.

slides.heading: The kilowatt hour
slides.body_md: The joule is too small for household use, so energy is sold in **kilowatt hours (kWh)**, called **units**. **1 kWh** is the energy used by a **1 kW** appliance in **1 hour**: $1\ \text{kWh} = 1000\ \text{W} \times 3600\ \text{s} = 3.6 \times 10^{6}$ J. Energy in kWh = **power in kW × time in hours**.

visual.alt: Graph of energy used, in kilowatt hours, against hours of use for three appliances. The two kilowatt heater line is steepest and reaches six units in three hours; the one hundred watt television line is nearly flat and reaches only point four units in four hours.
visual.caption: Energy in kWh = power in kW × time in hours: the slope of each line is the power.

slides.narration: A joule is a tiny amount of energy, so electricity companies count energy in kilowatt hours, which they call units. One kilowatt hour is the energy a one kilowatt appliance uses in one hour, which is three point six million joules. To find the units used, multiply the power in kilowatts by the time in hours.

slides.heading: Worked example: a monthly bill
slides.body_md:
**Problem.** A family uses an 80 W ceiling fan for 10 h a day, three 20 W LED tubes for 5 h a day and a 150 W refrigerator for 24 h a day. Find the energy used in 30 days and the cost at ₹6 per unit.

**Per day:** fan $0.08 \times 10 = 0.8$ kWh; tubes $3 \times 0.02 \times 5 = 0.3$ kWh; refrigerator $0.15 \times 24 = 3.6$ kWh; total $0.8 + 0.3 + 3.6 = 4.7$ kWh.

**30 days:** $4.7 \times 30 = 141$ kWh. **Cost:** $141 \times 6 = 846$, that is ₹846.

visual.alt: Table of daily and monthly energy for each appliance in the bill example

slides.narration: Change each power into kilowatts, then multiply by the hours. The fan uses point eight of a unit a day, the tube lights point three, and the refrigerator, running all day, three point six. That is four point seven units a day, or one hundred and forty one units a month. At six rupees a unit, the bill is eight hundred and forty six rupees.

slides.heading: Quick check: units used
slides.body_md: Find the energy in kilowatt hours.
slides.narration: Quick check. Multiply the power in kilowatts by the time in hours.

slides.heading: Saving energy at home
slides.body_md: An appliance’s energy use depends on **both** its power and its **hours of use**. A low-power device left on all day can use more than a high-power one used briefly. Efficient devices give the same output for less power: an LED lamp gives about as much light as an old filament bulb of several times its wattage.

headers: kWh in 30 days at 6 h a day

visual.alt: Table comparing the monthly energy of a filament bulb and an LED lamp used six hours a day

slides.narration: The units on a bill depend on power and on time. A small device that runs all day can cost more than a big one used for a few minutes. Efficient devices save energy. An LED lamp gives about the same light as a filament bulb that uses many times more power, so changing lamps cuts the bill noticeably.

slides.heading: Worked example: heater coils in series and in parallel
slides.body_md:
**Problem.** A room heater has two identical coils of 44 Ω. Find its power on 220 V with (a) one coil, (b) both coils in series, (c) both in parallel.

**(a)** $P = \dfrac{220 \times 220}{44} = 1100$ W.

**(b)** $R = 88$ Ω: $P = \dfrac{220 \times 220}{88} = 550$ W.

**(c)** $R = 22$ Ω: $P = \dfrac{220 \times 220}{22} = 2200$ W.

visual.alt: Table of the three settings of a two-coil room heater

slides.narration: With the voltage fixed, power is voltage squared over resistance. One coil gives eleven hundred watts. Two coils in series double the resistance and halve the power to five hundred and fifty watts. Two coils in parallel halve the resistance and double the power to twenty two hundred watts. That is how a heater’s low, medium and high settings work.

slides.heading: Quick check: comparing energy use
slides.body_md: Decide which appliance uses the most energy.
slides.narration: Quick check. Work out power in kilowatts times hours for each appliance before comparing.

slides.heading: Summary: Part 1
bullets: P = VI = I²R = V²/R (watt); 1 W = 1 J s⁻¹.
Rating “P watt, V volt”: converts P joules per second at V volts; R = V²/P, I = P/V.
At a fixed resistance, P ∝ V².
1 kWh = 3.6 × 10⁶ J; units = kW × hours; cost = units × rate.

visual.alt: Summary table of energy, power and cost

slides.narration: Let us sum up Part 1. Electrical energy is voltage times current times time, and power is the rate of using it, voltage times current. A power rating tells you the energy used each second at the stated voltage, and from it you can find the resistance. Household energy is counted in kilowatt hours, and the bill is units times the rate.

slides.heading: Exam tips: Part 1
bullets: Change watts to kilowatts and minutes to hours before finding kWh.
Find R from the rating first when the voltage changes; R stays the same.
For energy in joules, time must be in seconds.
State the meaning of a rating with the words “when connected to … volts”.

rows: Same power at a lower voltage

visual.alt: Table of three common slips in Part 1 and their fixes

slides.narration: Some tips. Before finding units, change watts into kilowatts and minutes into hours. If the voltage changes, first find the resistance from the rating, because the resistance stays the same. Use seconds when the answer is wanted in joules. And when you explain a rating, say that the power is converted only when the stated voltage is applied.

goals: Describe how power reaches a house and the order of the parts from the pole to the circuits
Explain why switches and fuses go in the live wire; choose a fuse rating; compare a fuse and an MCB
Describe the ring main system, the two-way switch and the three-pin plug
Explain earthing, the colour code and electrical safety precautions

slides.heading: From the power station to your socket
slides.body_md: Part 2 — how electricity travels to a house, how the house is wired, and what keeps the people inside safe.

rows: Carries a fault current safely to the ground

visual.alt: Table of four devices in the supply system and their jobs

slides.narration: Electricity is produced far away in a power station, carried across the country on tall towers, and finally reaches the sockets in your home. In this part we follow that journey, see how a house is wired, and learn the safety devices, the fuse, the circuit breaker and the earth wire, that protect people and appliances.

slides.heading: Power distribution
slides.body_md: Power is generated at about **11 kV**, **stepped up** to about **132 kV** (or more) and sent along transmission lines. At substations it is **stepped down** in stages — to **33 kV**, then **11 kV**, then to **220 V** at a local transformer — before it enters houses. Transmitting at a **high voltage** means a **small current** for the same power, so the heat lost in the lines, **I²R**, is far less.

visual.alt: Flow of electric power from the power station through step-up, transmission and step-down stages to houses

slides.narration: At the power station, electricity is produced at about eleven thousand volts. A transformer steps it up to a very high voltage for the long journey, because a high voltage means a small current, and a small current wastes little energy as heat in the wires. Near the town, it is stepped down in stages until it reaches homes at two hundred and twenty volts.

slides.heading: From the pole to the circuits
slides.body_md: In order: **pole** → **company fuse** (in the live wire, sealed) → **kWh meter** (records units) → **main switch** (double pole: cuts **both** live and neutral) → **distribution board** with a **fuse or MCB for each circuit**. Separate circuits: **lighting** (about 5 A), **power** (about 15 A, for geysers and heaters) and the **ring main**. All appliances are connected in **parallel**, so each gets 220 V and works independently.

slides.narration: The cable from the pole first passes the company fuse, which sits in the live wire. Next comes the kilowatt hour meter, then the main switch, which cuts off both the live and the neutral wires together. The distribution board then splits the supply into separate circuits, each with its own fuse or circuit breaker. Every appliance is joined in parallel.

slides.heading: Switch and fuse in the live wire
slides.body_md: A **fuse** is a short, thin wire of an alloy with a **low melting point** (such as tin and lead) joined **in series** in the **live wire**. If the current exceeds its rating, it **melts** and breaks the circuit. Switches and fuses go in the **live wire** so that, when the switch is off or the fuse has blown, the appliance is **disconnected from the high potential**. In the neutral wire, the appliance would stay live even when “off”.

slides.narration: A fuse is a thin wire that melts if too much current flows, breaking the circuit before the wiring overheats. Both the fuse and the switch must be in the live wire. Then, when the switch is off or the fuse has melted, the appliance is cut off from the live supply. If they were in the neutral wire, the appliance would still be live and could give a shock.

slides.heading: Worked example: choosing a fuse
slides.body_md:
**Problem.** Choose a suitable fuse, from 3 A, 5 A and 15 A, for (a) a 440 W mixer and (b) a 2.2 kW geyser, both on 220 V.

**(a)** $I = \dfrac{P}{V} = \dfrac{440}{220} = 2$ A: use the **3 A** fuse.

**(b)** $I = \dfrac{2200}{220} = 10$ A: use the **15 A** fuse.

**Rule:** choose the rating **just above** the normal current — a much larger fuse would not melt in time.

visual.alt: Table of normal currents and fuse ratings for a mixer and a geyser

slides.narration: Find the normal current first: power divided by voltage. The mixer draws two amperes, so a three ampere fuse suits it. The geyser draws ten amperes, so it needs the fifteen ampere fuse. Always choose the rating just above the normal current. A fifteen ampere fuse on the mixer would let a dangerous fault current flow without melting.

slides.heading: Quick check: fuse rating
slides.body_md: Choose the right fuse for an appliance.
slides.narration: Quick check. Work out the normal current, then pick the rating just above it.

slides.body_md: In a **ring main**, a cable carrying live, neutral and earth **starts at the distribution board, runs round the rooms and returns to the board**, protected by a **30 A fuse or MCB**. Sockets are connected **in parallel** at points on the ring. Because current reaches each socket **along two paths**, each part of the cable carries less current, so a **thinner cable** can be used, and new sockets are easy to add.

slides.heading: Worked example: will the MCB trip?
slides.body_md:
**Problem.** A kitchen circuit on 220 V is protected by a 20 A MCB. A 1200 W microwave, a 2000 W induction cooktop and a 320 W refrigerator are on. (a) Find the total current. (b) Will the MCB trip if a 1100 W kettle is also switched on?

**(a)** $P = 1200 + 2000 + 320 = 3520$ W; $I = \dfrac{3520}{220} = 16$ A.

**(b)** $I = \dfrac{3520 + 1100}{220} = 21$ A, which is more than 20 A, so the **MCB trips**.

visual.alt: Table of the kitchen loads, total power, current and whether the circuit breaker trips

slides.narration: Appliances in parallel each draw their own current, so add the powers first. Three thousand five hundred and twenty watts at two hundred and twenty volts is sixteen amperes, below the breaker’s rating. Adding the kettle raises the current to twenty one amperes, so the miniature circuit breaker trips and switches the circuit off. It can be switched on again once the load is reduced.

slides.heading: Two-way (staircase) switch
slides.body_md: A **two-way switch** has a **common terminal** and **two contacts**. For a staircase lamp, two such switches are used: the **live** wire goes to the common terminal of S1, two **strap wires** join the matching contacts of S1 and S2, and the common terminal of S2 goes to the **lamp**. The lamp is **on** when both levers rest on the **same** strap wire; flipping **either** switch turns it **off** (or on).

It is **thicker** so that it **cannot be pushed into the live or neutral hole** by mistake. The socket’s switch and fuse are in the live line.

slides.heading: Earthing
slides.body_md: **Earthing:** the **metal body** of an appliance is joined by the **earth wire** to a **copper plate buried deep in moist ground** (packed with charcoal and salt to keep the ground conducting). If the live wire touches the body, a **large current flows to earth** through this low-resistance path, the **fuse melts** (or the MCB trips) and the live supply is cut off. Without earthing, a person touching the body would complete the circuit and get a shock.

slides.narration: Earthing joins the metal body of an appliance to a copper plate buried in damp ground. If a live wire comes loose and touches the body, a very large current rushes to earth along this easy path. The fuse melts at once and the supply is cut off. Without an earth wire, the body would stay live, and anyone touching it could get a serious shock.

slides.heading: Colour code and safety precautions
slides.body_md: **Colour code (new international):** live — **brown**; neutral — **light blue**; earth — **green or green-yellow**. (Older wiring: live red, neutral black, earth green.) **Precautions:** use wires of the correct current rating; never replace a fuse by a thicker or copper wire; switch off the main switch before repairs; earth all metal-bodied appliances; do not overload sockets; never touch switches with wet hands; replace worn insulation at once.

visual.alt: Table of the colour code for live, neutral and earth wires with their normal potentials

slides.narration: Wires are colour coded so that electricians never mix them up. In the new code, the live wire is brown, the neutral is light blue, and the earth is green or green and yellow. Older houses used red, black and green. Simple habits keep us safe: switch off the mains before any repair, never overload a socket, and never touch switches with wet hands.

slides.heading: Summary: Part 2
bullets: Power is transmitted at high voltage (small current, small I²R loss) and stepped down to 220 V.
Pole → company fuse → kWh meter → main switch (double pole) → distribution board → circuits in parallel.
Fuse: low melting point, in series in the live wire, rating just above the normal current; MCB trips and can be reset.
Ring main: loop from and back to the board, 30 A, sockets in parallel, two paths.
Earth pin longer and thicker; earthing sends fault current to the ground; live brown, neutral light blue, earth green-yellow.

visual.alt: Summary table of protective devices, where they go and what they protect against

slides.narration: Let us sum up Part 2. Electricity is sent at high voltage to cut losses and reaches homes at two hundred and twenty volts. Inside, it passes the company fuse, the meter and the main switch to the distribution board. Fuses and switches go in the live wire. The ring main feeds sockets in parallel, and earthing protects us from a live metal body.

slides.heading: Exam tips: Part 2
bullets: Give the order from the pole exactly: company fuse, meter, main switch, distribution board.
For “why in the live wire?”, say the appliance is cut off from the high potential when off.
Fuse rating: calculate I = P ÷ V and choose the next rating above it.
For the earth pin, give both reasons: longer (first in, last out) and thicker (cannot enter L or N).

sections.heading: 1. Electrical energy and power
sections.body_md:
- Energy: $W = QV = VIt = I^{2}Rt = \dfrac{V^{2}t}{R}$ (joule). In a resistor it all becomes heat (Joule heating).
- Power: $P = \dfrac{W}{t} = VI = I^{2}R = \dfrac{V^{2}}{R}$ (watt; 1 W = 1 J s⁻¹; 1 kW = 1000 W; 1 MW = 10⁶ W).
- Use $I^{2}R$ when the current is common (series) and $V^{2}/R$ when the voltage is common (parallel, mains).

The power of an appliance that converts one joule of electrical energy every second.

sections.heading: 2. Power rating of an appliance
sections.body_md:
- **“1000 W, 220 V”**: when connected to 220 V the appliance converts 1000 J of electrical energy every second.
- From the rating: $I = \dfrac{P}{V}$ and $R = \dfrac{V^{2}}{P}$ (R stays the same if the voltage changes).
- On a different voltage: $P' = \dfrac{V'^{2}}{R}$, so $\dfrac{P'}{P} = \left(\dfrac{V'}{V}\right)^{2}$.
- For the same voltage, a higher-power appliance has a lower resistance.

key_terms.definition_md: The power an appliance converts when it is connected to its stated (rated) voltage.

visual.alt: Table of three power ratings with their current and resistance

sections.heading: 3. The kilowatt hour and electricity bills
sections.body_md:
- **1 kWh** = energy used by a 1 kW appliance in 1 hour $= 1000 \times 3600 = 3.6 \times 10^{6}$ J; the commercial **unit** of electrical energy.
- Units = power (kW) × time (h) × number of appliances × days.
- Cost = units × rate per unit.
- Energy use depends on power **and** hours of use; efficient devices (LED lamps) save units.

key_terms.definition_md: The electrical energy consumed by an appliance of power one kilowatt working for one hour; it equals 3.6 million joules.

visual.alt: Table of three ways of using one kilowatt hour

sections.heading: 4. Power distribution and house wiring
sections.body_md:
- Generated at about **11 kV** → stepped up to about **132 kV** → transmission lines → stepped down to **33 kV**, then **11 kV**, then **220 V** for houses. High voltage means low current, so less **I²R** loss in the lines.
- Supply in India: **220 V, 50 Hz** AC; live wire at 220 V, neutral at about 0 V.
- From the pole: **company fuse** (in the live wire) → **kWh meter** → **main switch** (double pole: breaks live and neutral) → **distribution board** (a fuse or MCB for each circuit) → circuits.
- Appliances are connected **in parallel**: each gets 220 V and can be switched independently.

key_terms.definition_md: The box after the main switch from which separate circuits, each with its own fuse or MCB, are taken to different parts of a house.
A switch that breaks both the live and the neutral wires at the same time.

visual.alt: Table of voltages at three stages of power distribution

sections.heading: 5. Fuse, MCB and the ring main
sections.body_md:
- **Fuse:** a short thin wire of an alloy of **low melting point** (tin–lead), joined **in series in the live wire**; it melts when the current exceeds its rating (overload or short circuit). Rating: **just above** the normal current $I = P/V$.
- **MCB (miniature circuit breaker):** an automatic switch that **trips** when the current is too large and can simply be **reset**.
- **Switches and fuses in the live wire:** when off or blown, the appliance is disconnected from the high potential.
- **Ring main:** a cable (L, N, E) runs from the distribution board round the rooms and **back to the board**; protected by a **30 A** fuse or MCB; sockets in **parallel**; current reaches each socket by **two paths**, so a thinner cable will do.

key_terms.definition_md: A safety device: a short wire of low melting point in the live wire that melts and breaks the circuit when the current exceeds a set value.
A household circuit in which a cable loop starting and ending at the distribution board feeds sockets connected in parallel along it.

formulas.label: Normal current, for choosing a fuse

visual.alt: Table comparing a fuse and a miniature circuit breaker

sections.heading: 6. Two-way switch, three-pin plug, earthing and safety
sections.body_md:
- **Two-way switch:** a common terminal and two contacts. Staircase wiring: live → common of S1; two strap wires join the contacts of S1 and S2; common of S2 → lamp → neutral. Lamp on when both levers are on the same strap; either switch changes it.
- **Three-pin plug:** earth pin **longer** (connects first, disconnects last) and **thicker** (cannot enter the L or N hole).
- **Earthing:** the metal body is joined to a copper plate buried in moist ground; a live-to-body fault sends a large current to earth, so the fuse melts.
- **Colour code (new):** live **brown**, neutral **light blue**, earth **green / green-yellow** (old: red, black, green).
- **Safety:** correct fuse rating, no overloading, switch off the mains for repairs, dry hands, earthed metal appliances, good insulation.

key_terms.definition_md: Connecting the metal body of an appliance to the earth through a thick wire and a buried plate, so that a fault current flows to the ground.
A switch with one common terminal that can be connected to either of two contacts, used in pairs to control one lamp from two places.

notes.exam_tips_md:
**Common mistakes**
- Using watts and minutes when finding kWh.
- Assuming an appliance gives its rated power on any voltage.
- Putting the fuse or switch in the neutral wire.
- Choosing a fuse rating far above the normal current.
- Giving only one reason for the shape of the earth pin.

**How marks are usually awarded**
- Bills: units per appliance (1), total units (1), cost (1).
- Wiring: correct order of parts and the function of each.
- Safety: a reason for each device, linked to the live wire or to earth.

questions.stem_md: A room heater is marked 2200 W, 220 V. The resistance of its element when working normally is:
questions.solution_md: $R = \dfrac{V^{2}}{P} = \dfrac{220 \times 220}{2200} = 22$ Ω — option (c).

questions.stem_md: A rice cooker rated 800 W, 220 V is used on a day when the supply falls to 176 V. Assuming its resistance does not change, its power is:
questions.solution_md: $P' = P \times \left(\dfrac{176}{220}\right)^{2} = 800 \times 0.64 = 512$ W — option (b).

questions.stem_md: A ceiling fan is marked “75 W, 220 V”. This means that the fan:

options.text_md: uses 75 J of energy every hour on any supply
can safely carry a current of at most 75 A
converts 75 J of electrical energy every second when connected to a 220 V supply
has a resistance of 75 Ω

questions.solution_md: Power is energy per second at the rated voltage — option (c).

questions.stem_md: A current I flows for a time t through a resistor R that has a p.d. V across it. Which expression does NOT give the electrical energy converted?

options.text_md: VIt
I²Rt
V²t/R
IRt

questions.solution_md: IR is a voltage, so IRt has the unit volt second, not joule; the other three are equal to W — option (d).

questions.stem_md: Heater coil A is rated 500 W, 220 V and coil B is rated 1000 W, 220 V. Which statement about their resistances is correct?

options.text_md: A has twice the resistance of B
B has twice the resistance of A
Both have the same resistance
A has four times the resistance of B

questions.stem_md: The 12 V battery of a parked car supplies 5 A to its headlights for 10 minutes. The electrical energy supplied is:
questions.solution_md: $W = VIt = 12 \times 5 \times 600 = 36000$ J — option (d).

questions.stem_md:
**Assertion (A):** A 2000 W heater has a lower resistance than a 1000 W heater made for the same voltage.

**Reason (R):** At a fixed voltage the power P = V²/R is inversely proportional to the resistance.

Choose the correct option.

options.text_md: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true, but R is false.
A is false, but R is true.

questions.solution_md: Both are true; since R = V²/P, doubling the power halves the resistance — option (a).

questions.stem_md: True or false? For a fixed current, the heat produced each second in a wire is directly proportional to its resistance.

options.text_md: True
False

questions.solution_md: True: heat per second is I²R, which is proportional to R when I is fixed.

questions.stem_md: One watt is the power of an appliance that converts one ___ of electrical energy every second.
questions.solution_md: **Joule** (1 W = 1 J s⁻¹).

questions.stem_md: The 60 Ω element of a soldering iron carries 2 A for 5 minutes. Find the heat produced, in kJ.
questions.solution_md: $H = I^{2}Rt = 2 \times 2 \times 60 \times 300 = 72000$ J, that is $H = 72$ kJ.

questions.stem_md: Find the resistance, in ohms, of the heating plate of a 550 W, 220 V sandwich maker when it works normally.
A microwave oven rated 1320 W is used on the 220 V mains. Find the current it draws, in amperes.
What does the marking “1.5 kW” on an electric kettle tell you?

answer.model_answer_md: Working at its rated voltage, the kettle converts 1500 joules of electrical energy into heat each second.

questions.solution_md: 1500 J per second at the rated voltage.

marking_scheme.step: Energy per second at rated voltage

questions.stem_md: An electric iron is rated 1100 W, 220 V. (a) Find the resistance of its element. (b) Find its power when the supply voltage falls to 198 V.
A halogen desk lamp is rated 110 W, 220 V. Calculate (a) its resistance when lit, (b) the current it draws and (c) the energy, in kWh, it uses in 5 hours.
A 500 W mixer-grinder is used for a total of 2 hours. The electrical energy it uses is:

options.text_md: 1000 kWh
1 kWh
250 kWh
0.25 kWh

questions.solution_md: Energy $= 0.5 \times 2 = 1$ kWh — option (b).

questions.stem_md: A 2 kW geyser is used for 30 minutes every day. At ₹7 per unit, the cost of running it for 30 days is:
questions.solution_md: Units $= 2 \times 0.5 \times 30 = 30$ kWh; cost $= 30 \times 7 = 210$, that is ₹210 — option (b).

questions.stem_md: Which of these uses the most electrical energy?

options.text_md: A 2000 W heater running for 15 minutes
A 60 W fan running for 10 hours
A 100 W television running for 4 hours
A 1000 W iron running for 20 minutes

questions.solution_md: Fan $0.06 \times 10 = 0.6$ kWh; heater $2 \times 0.25 = 0.5$ kWh; television $0.1 \times 4 = 0.4$ kWh; iron about 0.33 kWh — option (b).

questions.stem_md: The energy consumed by a 1 kW appliance working for one ___ is 1 kWh.
questions.solution_md: **Hour**.

questions.stem_md: The meter that records the electrical energy used in a house, in units, is called the ___ meter.
questions.solution_md: **Kilowatt hour** (kWh, energy) meter.

questions.stem_md: True or false? A 100 W lamp kept on for 10 hours uses one unit of electrical energy.

options.text_md: True
False

questions.solution_md: True: $0.1 \times 10 = 1$ kWh, which is one unit.

questions.stem_md: A 750 W water pump on a terrace runs for 2 hours a day. Find the energy it uses in 30 days, in kWh.
questions.solution_md: Energy $= 0.75 \times 2 \times 30 = 45$ kWh.

questions.stem_md: In a flat, a 1.5 kW air conditioner runs 4 hours a day, a 200 W television 3 hours a day and four 10 W LED bulbs 5 hours a day. At ₹8 per unit, find the cost, in rupees, for 30 days.
questions.solution_md: Daily: $1.5 \times 4 + 0.2 \times 3 + 4 \times 0.01 \times 5 = 6.8$ kWh; 30 days: $6.8 \times 30 = 204$ kWh; cost $= 204 \times 8 = 1632$, that is ₹1632.

questions.stem_md: A family’s solar panels supplied 2.5 kWh in a cloudy day. Express this energy in megajoules (1 MJ = 10⁶ J).
questions.solution_md: $2.5 \times 3.6 \times 10^{6} = 9 \times 10^{6}$ J, so the energy is $E = 9$ MJ.

questions.stem_md: Why is household electrical energy sold in kilowatt hours rather than in joules?

answer.model_answer_md: A joule is far too small: a single day’s use would run into millions of joules, so the larger kWh (3.6 × 10⁶ J) is convenient.

questions.solution_md: The joule is too small a unit.

questions.stem_md: A 1.2 kW washing machine is used for 45 minutes a day. Find (a) the energy it uses in 30 days and (b) the cost at ₹6.50 per unit.

A stationery shop replaces ten 40 W tube lights by ten 18 W LED tubes. The lights are on 10 hours a day. (a) How many units are saved in 30 days? (b) Why does the LED tube give about the same light for less power?

answer.model_answer_md: (a) Saving per tube $= 40 - 18 = 22$ W; units saved $= \dfrac{22 \times 10 \times 10 \times 30}{1000} = 66$ kWh. (b) An LED converts a much larger fraction of its electrical energy into light and wastes less as heat.

questions.solution_md: 66 kWh; more efficient.

questions.stem_md: A 660 W juicer is used on the 220 V mains. Which fuse is most suitable for it?

options.text_md: 5 A
1 A
2 A

questions.solution_md: $I = \dfrac{660}{220} = 3$ A, so the fuse must be rated a little above 3 A: 5 A. A 1 A or 2 A fuse would melt in normal use; a 30 A fuse would not protect — option (a).

questions.stem_md: Electricians place the switch and the fuse of every circuit in the live wire. The main reason is that:

options.text_md: the live wire carries more current than the neutral wire
the neutral wire is at a higher potential than the live wire
a fuse in the live wire uses less energy
when the switch is off or the fuse has blown, the appliance is cut off from the high potential of the supply

questions.solution_md: In the live wire, opening the circuit leaves the appliance at earth potential, so it is safe to touch — option (d).

questions.stem_md: In a new flat, rewireable fuses are replaced by miniature circuit breakers (MCBs). An MCB differs from a fuse because it:

options.text_md: must be replaced each time it operates
is connected in the neutral wire
never switches off a circuit
can simply be switched on again after it trips, once the fault is removed

questions.solution_md: An MCB is an automatic switch that is reset by hand — option (d).

questions.stem_md: In the ring main system of a house, the socket outlets are connected:

options.text_md: in series, one after another along a single cable
in parallel, each by a separate cable from the electric pole
in parallel, along a cable loop that starts and ends at the distribution board
in series with the main switch only

questions.solution_md: The ring leaves the board and returns to it; sockets are tapped off in parallel — option (c).

questions.stem_md: Power from a hydroelectric station is sent to a city 200 km away at 132 kV instead of 11 kV. This is done mainly to:

options.text_md: increase the current so that more power arrives
make the electricity flow faster along the lines
reduce the current, and so the heat lost in the transmission lines
change the alternating current into direct current

questions.solution_md: For the same power, P = VI: a higher V means a smaller I, and the loss I²R falls — option (c).

questions.stem_md: The main switch fitted after the electricity meter of a house is a double-pole switch. When it is turned off, it:

options.text_md: breaks both the live and the neutral wires at the same time
breaks only the neutral wire
breaks only the earth wire
connects the live wire to the earth wire

questions.solution_md: A double-pole switch opens both supply wires together — option (a).

questions.stem_md: Which is the correct order of parts, starting from the electric pole, in the supply to a house?

options.text_md: Company fuse, kWh meter, main switch, distribution board
kWh meter, company fuse, distribution board, main switch
Main switch, distribution board, kWh meter, company fuse
Distribution board, main switch, company fuse, kWh meter

questions.solution_md: The sealed company fuse comes first, then the meter, then the main switch, then the board — option (a).

questions.stem_md:
**Assertion (A):** A fuse wire is connected in series with the live wire of the circuit it protects.

**Reason (R):** A fuse wire is made of a material with a low melting point.

Choose the correct option.

options.text_md: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true, but R is false.
A is false, but R is true.

questions.solution_md: Both are true, but R explains why the fuse melts, not why it is placed in series in the live wire — option (b).

questions.stem_md:
**Assertion (A):** The cable of a ring main can be thinner than a single cable feeding the same sockets from one end.

**Reason (R):** In a ring main, current reaches each socket along two paths.

Choose the correct option.

options.text_md: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true, but R is false.
A is false, but R is true.

questions.solution_md: Both are true; sharing the current between two paths means each part of the cable carries less — option (a).

questions.stem_md:
**Assertion (A):** Electric power is transmitted over long distances at low voltage to reduce the energy lost.

**Reason (R):** The heat lost in a transmission line is I²R, where I is the current in the line.

Choose the correct option.

options.text_md: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true, but R is false.
A is false, but R is true.

questions.solution_md: A is false: power is sent at high voltage, so that the current, and the I²R loss, is small. R is true — option (d).

questions.stem_md: True or false? A miniature circuit breaker must be replaced with a new one every time it trips.

options.text_md: True
False

questions.solution_md: False: an MCB is reset by switching it on again after the fault is cleared.

questions.stem_md: The fuse of a circuit is always connected in the ___ wire.
questions.solution_md: **Live** wire.

questions.stem_md: In a ring main system, the ring circuit is usually protected by a fuse or MCB of ___ A.
A bedroom circuit on the 220 V mains is protected by a 16 A MCB. What is the largest total power, in watts, that can be switched on before it trips?
The same power is sent along a line first at 11 kV and then at 132 kV. (a) By what factor is the current reduced? (b) By what factor is the heat lost in the line reduced?

answer.model_answer_md: (a) $I = P/V$, so the current falls by $\dfrac{132}{11} = 12$ times. (b) Loss $= I^{2}R$, so it falls by $12 \times 12 = 144$ times.

questions.stem_md: An electrician wires the fuse of a kitchen circuit into the neutral wire. Explain the danger if the fuse then blows because of a fault.

answer.model_answer_md: The appliances stop working, but they are still joined to the live wire at 220 V. Anyone touching a faulty appliance, believing the circuit dead, can get an electric shock through the body to earth.

questions.solution_md: Appliance stays live.

questions.stem_md: List, in order from the electric pole, the four parts through which the mains supply passes before it reaches the circuits of a house. State the job of (a) the kWh meter and (b) the main switch.

answer.model_answer_md: Company fuse → kWh meter → main switch → distribution board. (a) The kWh meter records the electrical energy used, in units. (b) The main switch cuts off both the live and the neutral wires so that the whole house can be disconnected, for example during repairs.

questions.solution_md: Order; two jobs.

questions.stem_md: Name the device in a modern distribution board that switches off a circuit automatically on overload and can be reset.

answer.model_answer_md: A miniature circuit breaker (MCB).

questions.solution_md: MCB.

questions.stem_md: The earth pin of a three-pin plug is made longer than the live and neutral pins so that:

options.text_md: it carries the larger current of the appliance
the appliance is earthed before it connects to the live supply and stays earthed until after it disconnects
the plug stays firmly in the socket
it can be inserted into the live hole when the earth hole is blocked

questions.solution_md: Being longer, it enters first and leaves last — option (b).

questions.stem_md: In the new international colour code used for house wiring, the insulation of the live wire is:

options.text_md: brown
light blue
green or green-yellow
black

questions.solution_md: Live brown, neutral light blue, earth green-yellow — option (a).

questions.stem_md: A staircase lamp is controlled by two two-way switches, and it is now on. If either switch is flipped:

options.text_md: the lamp stays on unless both switches are flipped
the lamp goes off only if the lower switch is flipped
the fuse blows
the lamp goes off, whichever switch is flipped

questions.solution_md: The lamp is on only when both levers rest on the same strap wire; flipping either one breaks the path — option (d).

questions.stem_md: Inside a steel-bodied washing machine, a loose live wire touches the body. The body is properly earthed. What happens?

options.text_md: The machine keeps running and its body stays at 220 V
The current flows back through the neutral and nothing changes
A large current flows to earth and the fuse melts, cutting off the live supply
The earth wire melts instead of the fuse

questions.solution_md: The earth path has a very low resistance, so the fault current is large and the fuse blows — option (c).

questions.stem_md: The earth pin of a three-pin plug is also made thicker than the other two pins. This is so that:

options.text_md: it cannot be pushed into the live or the neutral hole of a socket by mistake
it has a high resistance
it melts first during a fault
it can carry the full load current

questions.solution_md: A thick pin fits only the large earth hole — option (a).

questions.stem_md:
**Assertion (A):** The metal body of an electric oven is connected to the earth wire.

**Reason (R):** The earth wire carries the working current of the oven during normal use.

Choose the correct option.

options.text_md: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true, but R is false.
A is false, but R is true.

questions.solution_md: A is true; R is false: in normal use the earth wire carries no current — it carries current only during a fault — option (c).

questions.stem_md: True or false? With a pair of two-way switches, a corridor lamp can be switched on or off from either end of the corridor.

options.text_md: True
False

questions.solution_md: True: flipping either two-way switch changes the state of the lamp.

questions.stem_md: True or false? In the new colour code, the earth wire has brown insulation.

options.text_md: True
False

questions.solution_md: False: brown is live; the earth wire is green or green-yellow.

questions.stem_md: To protect the user, the metal body of an electric iron is connected to the ___ wire.
questions.solution_md: **Earth** wire.

questions.stem_md: A staircase lamp is controlled from both floors using two ___ switches.
questions.solution_md: **Two-way** switches.

questions.stem_md: The live wire of a water cooler touches its metal body. The live wiring up to the fault has a resistance of 0.3 Ω and the earth path from the body has 0.7 Ω. Find the fault current, in amperes, on the 220 V mains.
questions.solution_md: $I = \dfrac{220}{0.3 + 0.7} = 220$ A, far more than any fuse rating, so the fuse melts at once.

questions.stem_md: State the colours of the live, neutral and earth wires in the new colour code.

answer.model_answer_md: Live: brown; neutral: light blue; earth: green or green-yellow.

questions.solution_md: Brown; light blue; green-yellow.

questions.stem_md: Explain how earthing protects a person using a room heater with a metal body if a loose live wire touches the body.

answer.model_answer_md: The body is joined by a thick earth wire to a buried plate, a path of very low resistance. When the live wire touches the body, a large current flows to earth through this path instead of through a person; it melts the fuse (or trips the MCB) and the live supply is cut off.

questions.solution_md: Low-resistance path; fuse blows.

questions.stem_md: Give two reasons for the special shape of the earth pin of a three-pin plug.

answer.model_answer_md: It is longer, so it connects to earth before the live and neutral pins connect and disconnects after them. It is thicker, so it cannot be fitted into the live or neutral hole by mistake.

questions.solution_md: Longer; thicker.

questions.stem_md: Rina’s family is moving into an old house. State four precautions they should take with the electrical wiring and appliances.

answer.model_answer_md: Use fuses of the correct rating and never replace them with thick copper wire; earth all metal-bodied appliances and use three-pin plugs; switch off the main switch before any repair; do not overload sockets with adaptors; replace worn or cracked insulation; never handle switches with wet hands.

questions.solution_md: Any four precautions.

questions.stem_md: A lamp on a staircase is to be controlled from the bottom and from the top of the stairs. (a) What kind of switch is used? (b) Describe how the two switches and the lamp are connected to the live and neutral wires. (c) State when the lamp is on.

answer.model_answer_md: (a) Two two-way switches. (b) The live wire goes to the common terminal of the first switch; the two contacts of the first switch are joined to the two contacts of the second switch by two strap wires; the common terminal of the second switch goes to the lamp, and the lamp to the neutral. (c) The lamp is on when both switch levers rest on the same strap wire; flipping either switch then turns it off.

questions.solution_md: Two-way switches; connections; condition.

questions.stem_md: Match each item in Column A with its function in Column B.

options.text_md: Fuse
MCB
Earth wire
kWh meter

match_right.text_md: Gives a fault current a safe path to the ground
Trips on overload and can be reset
Melts and breaks the circuit when the current is too large

questions.solution_md: Fuse → melts; MCB → trips and resets; earth wire → safe path to ground; kWh meter → records energy.

questions.stem_md: Match each item in Column A with the correct entry in Column B.

options.text_md: Electric power
Commercial unit of energy
Heat produced in a resistor
Resistance of a 1000 W, 220 V element

questions.solution_md: Power → watt; commercial unit → kWh; heat → I²Rt; 220² ÷ 1000 = 48.4 Ω.

questions.stem_md:
(a) Define electrical power and state its SI unit. Starting from P = VI, show that P = I²R and P = V²/R. [3]

(b) An electric kettle is rated 1210 W, 220 V. Find (i) the resistance of its element, (ii) the current it draws normally and (iii) its power when the supply is only 200 V. [3]

(c) A heater has two identical coils, each of resistance 55 Ω, and is used on 220 V. Find its power with (i) one coil, (ii) both coils in series and (iii) both coils in parallel. (iv) Which setting warms a room fastest? Give a reason. [4]

answer.model_answer_md:
(a) Electrical power is the electrical energy converted per second; SI unit the watt (W). Since $V = IR$, $P = VI = I \times IR = I^{2}R$; since $I = V/R$, $P = V \times \dfrac{V}{R} = \dfrac{V^{2}}{R}$.

(b) (i) $R = \dfrac{220 \times 220}{1210} = 40$ Ω. (ii) $I = \dfrac{1210}{220} = 5.5$ A. (iii) $P = \dfrac{200 \times 200}{40} = 1000$ W.

answer.model_answer_md:

(c) Fuses of 3 A, 5 A and 15 A are available. (i) Choose a fuse for a 330 W juicer. (ii) Choose a fuse for a 2.75 kW room heater. (iii) Why would a 15 A fuse be unsafe for the juicer? (iv) Why must a blown fuse never be replaced by a thick copper wire? [4]

answer.model_answer_md:
(a) A fuse is a short, thin wire that melts and breaks the circuit when the current exceeds a safe value. Its material (an alloy such as tin–lead) has a low melting point. It is connected in series in the live wire.

(b) (i) $1500 + 1800 + 660 = 3960$ W. (ii) $I = \dfrac{3960}{220} = 18$ A. (iii) $I = \dfrac{3960 + 1000}{220} \approx 22.5$ A, more than 20 A, so the MCB trips.

(c) (i) $I = \dfrac{330}{220} = 1.5$ A: the 3 A fuse. (ii) $I = \dfrac{2750}{220} = 12.5$ A: the 15 A fuse. (iii) A fault current of several amperes could overheat the juicer’s thin wires or start a fire without melting a 15 A fuse. (iv) Copper has a high melting point and a thick wire carries a large current without melting, so the circuit would have no protection.

(b) (i) Joining the metal body of an appliance to a plate buried in the earth through a thick wire. (ii) $I = \dfrac{220}{0.2 + 0.9} = 200$ A. (iii) This current is far above 15 A, so the fuse melts and cuts off the live supply.

The lamp is on when both levers are on the same strap wire. (ii) Live brown, neutral light blue, earth green or green-yellow. (iii) Switch off the main switch before a repair.
